definition.text: The largest total amount of carbon dioxide humanity can still emit, added up over time, while keeping global warming below a chosen limit.

facts.text: Counted from the pre-industrial year 1750 it is the total carbon budget; counted from a recent date it is the remaining carbon budget.
It is also called an emissions budget, quota or allowable emissions.
Global warming rises almost in a straight line with cumulative carbon dioxide emissions, which is what makes a budget meaningful.
The warming that results does not depend on where the emissions come from and depends little on when they happen.
From 1750 to 2019 about 2390 gigatonnes of CO2 had already been emitted worldwide.
Estimates depend on the temperature target, the chosen probability of staying below it, and how far other greenhouse gases are cut too.
A 2023 update found 250 GtCO2 left from January 2023 for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5 °C, about 6 years of current emissions.
For a 50% chance of staying below 2 degrees, the same update gave 1220 GtCO2, about 30 years of current emissions.

title: Allocating national carbon budgets

definition.text: The question of how to split the world's carbon budget among countries, which requires value judgments about fairness.

facts.text: Nations differ in population, industrialisation, past emissions and ability to cut emissions, so scientists use principles of equity to divide the budget.
Under 'common but differentiated responsibilities', countries that emitted more in the past or are richer get smaller budgets.
The egalitarian principle shares budgets by population, which raises the question whether individuals have a right to pollute.
Grandfathering shares budgets by each nation's emissions in a base year; it was used under the Kyoto Protocol and the early EU ETS and favours developed countries.
Recent work argues grandfathering is not a standard of equity because it builds biases against poorer states.

contested_note: Scholars disagree about which equity principle should divide the budget, and some reject grandfathering outright.

definition.text: Deliberate human activity that takes carbon dioxide out of the air and stores it durably on land, underground, in the ocean or in products.

facts.text: It is also called carbon removal, greenhouse gas removal or negative emissions.
Net zero needs deep emission cuts first and then removal as well; removal counterbalances emissions that are hard to eliminate, such as some from farming and aviation.
Methods include afforestation, reforestation, carbon farming, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, and direct air capture with storage.
Methods can be grouped by their place in the carbon cycle or by how long they store carbon, from decades to thousands of years.
As of 2023 about 2 gigatons of CO2 per year were removed, almost all by planting forests, equal to 4% of yearly human greenhouse gas emissions.
A 2019 NASEM report estimated that current safe and economic methods could remove up to 10 gigatons of CO2 per year if fully deployed.
Unlike removal, carbon capture and storage at a power plant cuts new emissions but does not lower the CO2 already in the air.

definition.text: How long carbon taken from the air stays stored before it might return to the atmosphere.

facts.text: Forests, kelp beds and other plants store carbon as they grow, but these stores are volatile because long-term storage cannot be guaranteed.
Wildfires, disease, economic pressure and changing politics can release stored carbon again.
Carbon can be stored more securely by injecting CO2 underground or locking it into insoluble carbonate salts.

definition.text: What it costs per tonne to remove carbon dioxide, which varies with how mature each method is and with the markets for removals and by-products.

facts.text: Direct air capture costs from $94 to $600 per tonne, biochar from $200 to $584, and nature-based solutions such as reforestation less than $50.
Biochar sells for more than nature-based removals because it stores carbon for hundreds or thousands of years, while forests are a more volatile store.
A direct air capture plant taking 1 MtCO2 a year uses 0.4–1.5 km2 of land, while roughly 46 million trees doing the same would need about 3,098–4,647 km2.
As of early 2023 financing fell short of what high-tech removal would need, and most new money came from voluntary private initiatives.
Concern exists because voluntary markets have historically been far smaller than markets created by government policy.

title: Carbon removal as moral hazard

definition.text: The worry that promises of future carbon removal could weaken efforts to cut emissions now.

facts.text: Critics stress that removal must not be treated as a substitute for cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
In 2018 relying on large-scale removal was seen as a major risk to the 1.5 °C goal, given uncertainty about how fast it can grow.
Removal plans in countries' 2023 climate pledges would need 1.2 billion hectares, as much land as all the world's cropland.
A 2019 NASEM report said that delaying mitigation because removal will provide a backstop misrepresents its real capacity.

contested_note: Critics see reliance on future removal as a risk that delays emission cuts, while it is also described as a needed complement for hard-to-abate sectors.

title: Marine carbon dioxide removal
article: Carbon dioxide removal#Marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR)

definition.text: Methods that remove carbon dioxide through the ocean, whose dissolved carbon stays in balance with CO2 in the air.

facts.text: Ocean alkalinity enhancement dissolves minerals such as olivine or limestone so that carbonate settles on the sea floor, at an estimated US$100 to $150 per tonne.
Electrochemical methods can strip carbonate from seawater and are much cheaper when combined with desalination.
Ocean fertilization would store carbon for only 10–100 years.
